summary:
Cajamarca has no documented trans-specific departmental law, ordinance, court ruling or incident series in the source inventory. The binding framework for trans visitors and residents of Cajamarca is Peru's national legislation, and none of the sources examined contains Cajamarca-specific content.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity. Its national Congress has nonetheless legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, removed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody situations and for cases where entry is required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The trigger recorded for the bills was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport. The dictamen then went to the plenary: on 2 April 2025 Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes and waived a second vote. Its Article 5.1 prohibits entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than one's birth sex.

Human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. Activist Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, argues that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so a visitor whose documents do not match their presentation has no quick national route to resolving the mismatch.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; among the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. The perpetrators were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. In February 2023 Rubi Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 bathroom provision does not meet on IDEHPUCP's reading. The same institute recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The restriction reaches private and public life. A national consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that assigned bathroom use by the sex recorded in the DNI (SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, concerning SmartFit). On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. Recorded hate-crime figures are themselves an undercount: co-author Gianna Camacho stresses that the published figures are only a sub-registry.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cajamarca live under the same national document regime as visitors: gender-identity recognition in Peru is long, costly and invasive, and no departmental procedure or legal-aid pathway for it appears in the sources.

Residents who encounter restroom exclusion can lodge a discrimination complaint with the national consumer-protection body, but the only sourced outcome of such a route is a dismissal (Resolution 0735-2022). No departmental body in Cajamarca is identified in the sources as handling gender-identity complaints.

The April 2025 law binds venues within Cajamarca as elsewhere: entry to sex-designated public sanitary facilities is determined by birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody and accompanied minors, elderly people and people with disabilities, and venues are obliged not to post ambiguous restroom signs.

National health guidance no longer uses pathologising terminology for gender diversity following the June 2024 revision, which affects how trans patients are treated in healthcare settings, though the sources do not describe departmental facility-level practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source records whether Article 5.1 has been enforced, contested or ignored in Cajamarca, and no incident of restroom exclusion or DNI-checking by security staff in the department is documented in the inventory.

Unresolved: the sources contain no figures for killings or rights violations of trans people recorded in Cajamarca between 2020 and 2023; the national totals published by the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI are not broken down by department.

Not sourced: whether any departmental ordinance, regional council measure or municipal resolution in Cajamarca addresses gender identity, and whether any local institution provides gender-affirming healthcare or legal representation for trans residents.

Not sourced: whether the state's crime-registration systems have been updated since the finding that sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from them, which currently prevents hate-crime prosecution.
